newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Africans say they must lead continental peace effort.
newsitem.headline: Africans say they must lead continental peace effort.

text.p: A U.S.-led plan for an all-Africa intervention force met another hurdle on Monday with Southern African foreign ministers expressing caution or strong reservations about the peacekeeping initiative.

Kaire Mbuende, executive secretary of the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC), told reporters that foreign ministers meeting their counterparts from the European Union had criticised the plan.
"The message the ministers are passing around is that the initiative must be from Africa and that they...are cautious and some have strong reservations on the U.S. proposal," he said.

Southern African ministers had not yet formally discussed the proposed 10,000-strong African Crisis Reaction Force, but most appeared to support the position adopted by South African President Nelson Mandela.
Mandela told U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher at the weekend that the project should not be seen as coming from one country, but rather through a body such as the United Nations.

Irish Foreign Minister and president of the EU Council of Ministers Dick Spring told Monday's start of the two-day SADC-EU conference that the EU would respect African leadership in resolving conflicts on the continent.
He welcomed the recent establishment of an SADC body charged with ensuring peace and stability in the region.
"A central element of its approach in this regard is the principle of African leadership in the resolution of its own conflicts," he said.
Spring also welcomed an African summit at the weekend to discuss the crisis in Burundi, which has been hobbled by sanctions since Tutsi military strongman Pierre Buyoya seized power on July 25.
He said the EU hoped regional action might bring about talks between Buyoya's army-appointed government and Hutu rebels fighting a fierce civil war.
SADC member Tanzania has largely led regional action on Burundi.
The other SADC members are Angola, Botswana, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Lesotho, Swaziland, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Mbuende also said southern African countries were prepared to contribute to efforts to ensure lasting peace in Bosnia.
"We have been alive to our international obligations by sending peacekeeping forces to different parts of the world," he said.
"However, we are not only a physical force to be present on the international scene...We are also an intellectual force capable of handling delicate negotiations and mediations," he added.
